sections.heading: What are the symptoms and triggers of asthma?
sections.body:
The main symptoms of asthma are problems with breathing. These include wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath and a tight chest. They may be worse at night and early in the morning. Symptoms happen when the airways become swollen.

Asthma + Lung UK describes needing the blue reliever inhaler often as a red flag. The charity says to see a GP as soon as possible in that situation. The need for a quicker review is a sign that asthma may not be well controlled.

The NHS says it is not fully understood what causes asthma. Possible risk factors include allergies, being born prematurely, and childhood exposure to air pollution or cigarette smoke. Common triggers include animal dander, dust mites, cold weather, pollution, physical activity, mould, pollen and respiratory infections.

Substances in some workplaces can also trigger symptoms, which is called occupational asthma. Doctors describe severe asthma in groups based on markers measured in the body. Severe eosinophilic asthma is marked by high levels of eosinophils in the airways. Eosinophils are a type of white blood cell. Severe allergic asthma shows high levels of IgE, which reflects a strong response to allergens. Non-eosinophilic severe asthma shows no high eosinophil levels.

sections.heading: How is asthma diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP or nurse will ask questions and listen to the chest. A simple breathing test may be used to check for signs of asthma, and sometimes a blood test. Specific tests include FeNO, spirometry and peak flow testing. Spirometry measures how much air a person can blow out and how fast. Peak flow testing records how fast a person can blow air out, usually at home over a period of time.

UK guidance for adults and young people starts with blood eosinophils or a FeNO test. If asthma is not confirmed that way, the next step is spirometry with a bronchodilator reversibility test. Peak flow readings over time are used when spirometry is unavailable or delayed. For children aged 5 to 16, FeNO comes first, followed by spirometry. The pathway does not cover children under 5.

FeNO is not available in every GP surgery, so spirometry or peak flow may be used instead. Spirometry is generally preferred over peak flow because it shows airflow obstruction more clearly and depends less on effort.

sections.heading: What are the treatments for asthma?
sections.body:
Inhalers are the main treatment for asthma. Reliever inhalers are used to treat symptoms when they occur, while preventer inhalers are taken daily. A preventer reduces inflammation in the airways. A reliever does not treat the asthma itself, only the symptoms it causes.

Most people with asthma are prescribed two types of inhaler. Some people use one combination inhaler for both jobs, called an anti-inflammatory reliever. The latest guidelines do not recommend giving anyone with asthma only a blue reliever inhaler. Anyone who has only a reliever should also have a steroid preventer.

The NHS says tablets and other treatments may be needed if asthma is severe. Biologic medicines used in severe asthma include some that target IgE and others that target the IL-5 pathway. In clinical trials, biologics reduced attacks and the need for steroid tablets. Serious allergic reactions to these medicines are rare but can be life-threatening.

sections.heading: Living with asthma: self-care, complications and outlook
sections.body:
The NHS lists helpful steps such as always having an inhaler to hand and using inhalers as the care team recommends. It also lists avoiding triggers, exercising regularly, keeping to a healthy weight and having vaccinations such as the flu vaccine.

An asthma action plan is a written guide to daily medicines, worsening symptoms and asthma attacks. Its sections are green for everyday care, amber for feeling worse and red for an asthma attack. An action plan helps people manage their asthma and lowers the risk of an asthma attack.

Asthma + Lung UK says everyone with asthma should have regular asthma reviews. At a review, a clinician can update the plan, check inhaler technique and confirm the medicines are right.

Repeated or continuous courses of steroid tablets are linked to complications such as fractures from thin bones and pneumonia. Long-standing inflammation can also cause changes in the airways. Some people with long-term severe asthma can develop COPD alongside their asthma. Most people with asthma can lead a normal life with proper self-care and medical treatment.

Living with severe asthma is linked to some risks, including a lower life expectancy in one source.

sections.heading: What happens in an asthma attack, and when should I call 999?
sections.body:
The NHS describes an asthma attack as severe symptoms and difficulty breathing, which can be life-threatening. The NHS advises sitting up straight and trying to keep calm while taking puffs of the reliever inhaler. It says to call 999 if symptoms get worse at any point, do not improve after the maximum reliever dose, or there is no inhaler.

NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe breathing difficulty, such as struggling to speak without pausing. It also lists lips or skin turning pale, blue or grey. NHS 111 Wales adds that 999 is needed if a person is too breathless to speak, eat or sleep, or the reliever is not helping.

If symptoms settle and 999 is not needed, the advice is still to see a GP or asthma nurse soon. NHS 111 is the route when it is unclear which service is needed.

faqs.a: The sources describe no cure for asthma. Most people with asthma can lead a normal life with proper self-care and medical treatment. Inhalers are the main treatment, and a written action plan helps lower the risk of an asthma attack. A clinician decides which treatment suits each person.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a reliever and a preventer inhaler?
faqs.a: A reliever inhaler treats symptoms when they occur. A preventer inhaler is taken daily and reduces inflammation in the airways. Asthma + Lung UK says a reliever does not treat the asthma itself, only the symptoms it causes. Most people with asthma are prescribed two types of inhaler.

faqs.q: What tests are used to diagnose asthma?
faqs.a: A GP or nurse asks questions and listens to the chest. The NHS says a simple breathing test may be used, and sometimes a blood test. Specific tests include FeNO, spirometry and peak flow testing. FeNO is not available in every GP surgery, so spirometry or peak flow may be used instead.

faqs.q: What is an asthma action plan?
faqs.a: An asthma action plan is a written guide to daily medicines, worsening symptoms and asthma attacks. Its sections are green for everyday care, amber for feeling worse and red for an asthma attack. The plan helps people manage their asthma and lowers the risk of an asthma attack. A clinician can update it at an asthma review.

faqs.q: When does an asthma attack need a 999 call?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 during an attack if symptoms get worse at any point. It also says to call 999 if there is no improvement after the maximum reliever dose, or if there is no inhaler. NHS inform lists struggling to speak without pausing, and pale, blue or grey lips or skin, as emergency signs. If a person is unsure which service they need, NHS 111 is the route.
